design_detail: Naturalistic within-person comparison, pooled from three studies at one university: 52 young drivers each drove a 20-minute simulated commute (STISIM fixed-base simulator, mixed rural and urban route with hazards and a divided-attention task) on the morning after a self-chosen night of social drinking and on a morning after no alcohol, in counterbalanced order. Drinking was not observed or assigned. After testing, participants were split by morning breath alcohol into a zero group (n = 26) and a residual-alcohol group (n = 26). Outcomes: 15 driving variables, NASA Task Load Index (workload) and the Alcohol Hangover Severity Scale.
can_establish: Whether the same young drivers drove worse in a demanding simulator on the morning after a night of social drinking than after a night without alcohol, including those whose breath alcohol was zero, and how they rated their own workload.
cannot_establish: Whether the impairment is due to alcohol itself rather than shorter or poorer sleep, the night out or expectation (sleep was not recorded, drinking amounts are not reported, and nobody was blind to condition); how it compares with legal blood alcohol limits (no alcohol-dose benchmark was run in this study); whether it applies to older or experienced drivers or to real roads; and whether residual alcohol adds risk (the residual and zero groups were formed after the fact and already differed on the control day).

sample.recruitment: Students and other people recruited through the experimenters' contacts, University of the West of England; unpaid; data from three studies with separate ethics approvals combined.
sample.inclusion_exclusion: Driving licence holders aged 18 to 25 with 1 to 6 years of driving experience, self-reported good health, not pregnant, not using illicit drugs, non-smokers, fewer than 5 caffeinated drinks a day, social drinkers who reported having hangovers regularly; a short familiarization drive screened for simulator sickness.
sample.demographics: Mean age 20.9 years (range 18 to 25); 21 men and 31 women.
sample.attrition: Not reported: no drop-outs, exclusions or missing data are described, and how many people were enrolled across the three studies is not given.
sample.selection_effects: Young, inexperienced drivers who drink socially and often have hangovers; participants chose the drinking night and could postpone a test morning depending on whether they had drunk, so the hangover mornings were self-selected. The split into zero and residual groups depended on how much and how late people drank.

exposure.measurement: Self-reported night of social drinking, recalled with a retrospective diary (some could not recall amounts); breath alcohol measured with a Lion Alcometer immediately before driving, with readings hidden from participants; hangover severity rated on the Alcohol Hangover Severity Scale after the drive.
exposure.dose_frequency_duration_route: Study conditions: drinks and amounts chosen by participants and not reported. Morning breath alcohol in the residual group averaged 0.047% (range 0.01 to 0.08%); all 52 had zero breath alcohol after the no-alcohol night. Mean hangover severity 4.7 (SD 1.8) on a 0 to 10 scale; 5.1 in the zero group and 4.3 in the residual group.
exposure.polysubstance: Illicit drug use and smoking excluded at screening (self-report); caffeine withheld on test mornings until after testing; other drug use on the drinking night not recorded.
exposure.abstinence_at_testing: Half the sample had zero breath alcohol at testing; the other half had residual alcohol up to 0.08%. Breath readings were not confirmed in blood, which the authors note may misclassify some participants.

comparison.controls: The same participants on a morning after no alcohol (all with zero breath alcohol).
comparison.matching: Within-person; condition order and driving-scenario order counterbalanced, although participants could rearrange test days.
comparison.unmeasured_premorbid: Sleep on both nights, time drinking ended, food and how much was drunk were not recorded or not reported; the authors name sleep loss as a likely part of the effect.
comparison.controls_other_drug_use: Not applicable within person; other drug use on the drinking night not recorded.

outcomes.instruments: STISIM Drive simulator, 60,000-foot scenario (about 20 minutes, 50 mph limit, UK road layout) recording divided attention (response time and its variability, correct, incorrect and missed responses), vehicle control (mean speed and speed variability, mean lane position, lane deviation, centre-line crossings, time off road, lane excursions) and violations (accidents and collisions, speed-limit exceedances, tickets such as failing to stop or running red lights); NASA Task Load Index (six dimensions, 0 to 100); Alcohol Hangover Severity Scale (12 symptoms rated 0 to 10), with fatigue analysed separately.
outcomes.validity_norms: The authors describe the one-hour highway test and its standard deviation of lateral position as the reference standard for driving impairment; this shorter urban scenario has no published benchmark against blood alcohol levels.
outcomes.operationalization: Impairment means a significant difference in the poorer direction between the hangover and control mornings on a paired comparison, after a significant MANOVA and ANOVA; effect sizes as Cohen's d.
outcomes.multiplicity_correction: MANOVA gating before separate ANOVAs and paired tests; no correction across the 15 driving variables and 6 workload dimensions; correlations shown only if p < 0.01 with nonparametric support, from an unreported number tested.
outcomes.assessor_blinding: Simulator measures were recorded automatically; participants and experimenters knew which morning was which; participants did not see their breath readings.

analysis.effect_sizes: Combined group (n = 52), hangover against control, means (SD): divided-attention response time 3.5 (1.8) against 2.4 (1.3), d = 0.55; incorrect responses 0.2 against 0.0, d = 0.21; missed responses 2.1 against 1.1, d = 0.30; mean speed 35.9 against 31.7 mph, d = 0.42; centre-line crossings 7.8% against 4.0%, d = 0.36; time off road 1.6% against 0.6%, d = 0.68; lane excursions 18.9 against 10.6, d = 0.58; tickets 1.2 against 0.8, d = 0.34. Not significant: response-time variability, correct responses, speed variability, mean lane position, lane deviation (2.9 against 2.6), accidents (1.8 against 1.3), speed exceedances. Zero group (n = 26): response time d = 0.69, mean speed d = 0.40, centre-line crossings d = 0.48, time off road d = 0.61, lane excursions d = 0.64; accidents 1.1 against 1.6 (not significant). Residual group (n = 26): response time d = 0.50, mean speed d = 0.45, time off road d = 0.72, excursions d = 0.51, accidents 2.5 against 0.9, d = 0.74. Workload (NASA-TLX overall) 53.8 against 38.4, d = 0.99. Multivariate effect of alcohol on driving F(1,50) = 19.4, p < 0.0001.
analysis.covariates: Gender and study entered as exploratory factors and dropped after non-significant multivariate tests; no other covariates.
analysis.preregistration_detail: No registration or protocol is mentioned.
analysis.selective_reporting: All 15 driving variables are tabulated. The correlations between self-ratings and driving are shown only when significant at p < 0.01 with nonparametric support, without the number tested, and it is not stated whether they used hangover-morning scores or differences from the control morning. The abstract does not mention that lane deviation, the measure closest to the reference standard, did not change.
analysis.power: Not reported; 26 per group for the residual comparison.

interpretation_gap.results_show: On the morning after a night of social drinking, the same young drivers responded more slowly to a divided-attention task, drove faster, crossed the centre line and left the road more often, made more lane excursions and collected more tickets in a 20-minute simulated commute than after a night without alcohol, with small to medium effects (d 0.21 to 0.68), while lane deviation, speed variability and accidents did not differ overall. The pattern was similar in the 26 whose breath alcohol was zero. They also rated the drive as needing more effort and workload. The residual group drove faster and got more tickets than the zero group on both mornings, not only after drinking.
interpretation_gap.claimed: The abstract and Conclusions state that the impairment reflects that seen with alcohol-impaired driving and was comparable to driving with a blood alcohol level at or above the legal limit used in several countries, even with zero breath alcohol. Gaps: (1) no alcohol-dose benchmark was run in this study; the comparison rests on another study (Mets et al., 2011) of a highway test whose main measure, lane deviation, did not change here; (2) the Results state that residual alcohol resulted in faster driving, more speed exceedances and more tickets, but Table 1 shows the residual group already drove faster (34.3 against 29.1 mph), exceeded speed limits more (10.4 against 7.0) and got more tickets (1.0 against 0.6) on the no-alcohol morning, with no alcohol-by-group interaction for these measures, so the difference is between people, not an effect of residual alcohol; (3) a lack of awareness of impairment is inferred from a few correlations selected by significance that differ between groups; (4) the effect is attributed to hangover although sleep was not recorded, which the authors acknowledge.

timeline.event: Laurell and Törnros: impaired vehicle control on a hangover morning in a naturalistic driving study (summarized in Gunn et al., 2018).

Verster et al.: greater weaving (standard deviation of lateral position) on a one-hour simulated highway drive during hangover, mostly in the second half (as described in this paper and in Gunn et al., 2018); Verster is a co-author of this paper.
Gunn et al. systematic review: driving studies too different to pool; two of three found impaired vehicle control.

Robbins et al.: student drivers the morning after drinking drove faster and exceeded limits longer in a 15-minute simulator test, mostly with residual alcohol, without impaired visual attention (as described in this paper).
This study: impairment on a 20-minute urban commute, also in participants with zero breath alcohol.

replication.where_it_stands: Several simulator and naturalistic studies, from overlapping and independent groups, report poorer driving the morning after drinking, but the measures differ: weaving on a long highway drive in one, lane excursions, time off road and speed on a short urban drive here, where weaving itself did not change. None has measured sleep alongside driving, and none links the urban-route measures to blood alcohol levels in the same scenario.

what_would_settle_it: A randomized crossover study in which the same drivers drink a measured amount of alcohol or a placebo, with sleep held equal and recorded, then drive the same urban scenario at zero blood alcohol (confirmed in blood) the next morning, with a third session at a known blood alcohol level on the same scenario to calibrate the size of any impairment, in drivers of different ages and experience.

domains.note: The within-person comparison removes stable differences between people, and both tests were in the morning with caffeine withheld. Sleep, food and the night out itself were not recorded and travel with the hangover. For the zero-versus-residual contrast the risk is high: the groups formed after the fact already differed in speed, speeding and tickets on the control morning.

Drinking was self-reported and unobserved, amounts are not reported and some could not recall them; residual alcohol by breath only. Zero alcohol after the control night was confirmed by breath test, and hangover severity was rated.

Volunteers from students and the experimenters' contacts who report regular hangovers; participants chose and could postpone their test mornings; three studies combined without describing how many were enrolled.
None; participants did not drive or ride to the university after drinking.
No information on drop-outs or exclusions across the three studies; consumption data are missing for some participants.
Driving measures were recorded automatically, but participants knew their condition, which may affect effort and motivation; workload and hangover ratings were given after the drive.

All driving variables are tabulated, but 21 outcomes were tested without correction and nothing was preregistered. The correlations between self-ratings and driving were selected by significance from an unreported number of tests and are at high risk.

risk_of_bias.reasoning: For the main within-person contrast (driving after a night of social drinking against after no alcohol), the design is reasonably protected: same people, counterbalanced order, automatic measures and all driving variables reported. What remains uncertain is attribution, since sleep and drinking amounts were not recorded and nobody was blind, and the result describes a night out drinking, not alcohol alone. The card may be cited for poorer simulated driving and higher workload the morning after drinking, including at zero breath alcohol. It should not be cited for an effect of residual alcohol (the groups differed already on the control morning), for equivalence with a blood alcohol level (not measured here), or for a lack of awareness of impairment (selected correlations).

key_findings.finding: Combined group (n = 52): on the hangover morning, divided-attention response time was slower (3.5 s, SD 1.8, against 2.4, SD 1.3; d = 0.55), with more incorrect (d = 0.21) and missed (d = 0.30) responses; mean speed was higher (35.9 against 31.7 mph; d = 0.42), centre-line crossings (7.8% against 4.0%; d = 0.36), time off road (1.6% against 0.6%; d = 0.68) and lane excursions (18.9 against 10.6; d = 0.58) increased, and tickets rose (1.2 against 0.8; d = 0.34). Eight of the 15 driving variables differed.
key_findings.locator: Table 1, Combined Groups columns; Results › 3.1 Driving Performance, 2nd and 4th paragraphs
key_findings.note: The printed d values cannot be reproduced from the table means and SDs with a simple pooled SD (for example 0.70 against the printed 0.55 for response time; editors' calculation), presumably because the method accounts for the within-person correlation, which is not reported; most printed values are smaller.

key_findings.finding: Lane deviation (2.9 against 2.6), speed variability, mean lane position, response-time variability, correct responses, accidents (1.8 against 1.3) and speed-limit exceedances did not differ significantly between hangover and control mornings in the combined group.

Zero breath alcohol group (n = 26): response time slower (3.4 against 2.3; d = 0.69), faster driving (33.7 against 29.1 mph; d = 0.40), more centre-line crossings (6.0% against 3.8%; d = 0.48), time off road (1.3% against 0.5%; d = 0.61) and lane excursions (20.2 against 9.7; d = 0.64); accidents 1.1 against 1.6 (not significant); incorrect and missed responses and tickets not significant.
key_findings.locator: Table 1, Zero BAC Group columns; Results › 3.1, 4th paragraph

key_findings.finding: Residual alcohol group (n = 26, with alcohol still measurable in the breath; values in the exposure field): response time slower (d = 0.50), faster driving (d = 0.45), more time off road (d = 0.72) and excursions (d = 0.51), and more accidents and collisions (2.5 against 0.9; d = 0.74), the only measure with an alcohol-by-group interaction.
key_findings.locator: Results › 3 (opening paragraph); Table 1, Residual Alcohol Group columns; Results › 3.1, 3rd paragraph

key_findings.finding: On the no-alcohol control morning the residual group already drove faster than the zero group (34.3 against 29.1 mph), exceeded speed limits more often (10.4 against 7.0) and got more tickets (1.0 against 0.6); the authors' significant group contrasts for speed (F(1,50) = 4.28), exceedances (F(1,50) = 4.59) and tickets (F(1,50) = 4.17) are main effects of group, not interactions with drinking.
key_findings.locator: Table 1, Control columns of the Zero BAC and Residual Alcohol groups; Results › 3.1, 2nd paragraph (last two sentences)
key_findings.note: Editors' reading of Table 1: the group difference is present without alcohol, so it reflects differences between people rather than an effect of residual alcohol.

key_findings.finding: Perceived workload rose on the hangover morning: NASA-TLX overall 53.8 (SD 13.6) against 38.4 (12.8), d = 0.99; effort 60.5 against 41.6, d = 0.80; all six dimensions significant (for example temporal demand F(1,50) = 37.8).
key_findings.locator: Table 1, Subjective Assessments rows; Results › 3.2 Subjective Measures, 2nd paragraph

key_findings.finding: Mean hangover severity was 4.7 (SD 1.8) on the 0 to 10 scale (5.1 in the zero group, 4.3 in the residual group); some participants could not recall how much they had drunk, and amounts are not reported; sleep was not recorded.

Correlations between self-ratings and driving (selected at p < 0.01): in the combined group lower hangover ratings went with faster driving (r = −0.359) and lower fatigue ratings with faster driving (r = −0.460); the associations differed between the zero and residual groups, and hangover ratings were not associated with workload ratings.
key_findings.locator: Table 2; Results › 3.3 Associations Between Measures, 1st and 3rd paragraphs

reporting_issues.issue: The Results state that residual alcohol resulted in greater speed, more speed exceedances and more tickets, but Table 1 shows these group differences on the no-alcohol control morning too, and no alcohol-by-group interaction is reported for them.
reporting_issues.consequence: The residual-alcohol effect on speeding and tickets is not supported; claims must not cite it.

reporting_issues.issue: The abstract and Conclusions equate the impairment with driving at or above a blood alcohol level used as a legal limit in several countries, but no blood alcohol benchmark was tested in this study; the comparison cites a highway-test study (Mets et al., 2011) whose main measure, lane deviation, did not change here.
reporting_issues.page: PMC HTML, Abstract; Discussion, 1st paragraph; 5. Conclusions; Table 1
reporting_issues.consequence: The equivalence to a blood alcohol level is an extrapolation, not a finding.

reporting_issues.issue: For the group contrast in speed-limit exceedances, F(1,50) = 4.59 is printed with partial eta squared 0.10; that F gives 0.084 (editors' calculation), and the same F appears for accidents and collisions.
reporting_issues.consequence: Probably a copying error; the statistic for exceedances is uncertain.

reporting_issues.issue: Alcohol consumption was collected with a retrospective diary but not reported, and the number of participants enrolled, excluded or lost across the three combined studies is not given.
reporting_issues.consequence: The exposure cannot be described in amounts and attrition cannot be assessed.

reporting_issues.issue: The method behind the printed Cohen's d values is not reproducible from the table: a simple pooled-SD calculation gives different values for most variables (for example 1.17 against the printed 0.99 for overall workload; editors' calculation).
reporting_issues.consequence: Effect sizes should be quoted as printed and described as the authors' calculation.

reporting_issues.issue: Whether the correlations in Table 2 used hangover-morning scores or differences from the control morning is not stated, nor how many correlations were tested before selecting those with p < 0.01.
reporting_issues.consequence: The lack-of-awareness interpretation cannot be evaluated.
